newsitem.title: FRANCE: Traders want tougher EU stance on wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: Traders want tougher EU stance on wheat exports.

text.p: European grain exporters said on Friday that unless the EU starts competing against cheaper wheat supplies from Argentina, Australia and Canada, it could lose some traditional markets.
"If they do not react, we are at a dead end," one trader said.
Exporters have repeatedly urged the EU to stop pricing its wheat against United States supplies, arguing that U.S. wheat was now out of step with world markets.
They particularly fear competition from Argentine wheat which is already making headway in eastern Europe and north Africa, traditional outlets for the EU.
But the EU, eager to avoid a new trade dispute with the U.S., has been careful to keep the level of its wheat subsidy as low as possible.
On Thursday the EU granted the export of 198,900 tonnes of EU wheat at a refund of 18 Ecus per tonne, valuing EU wheat for late December-early January at around $154 per tonne fob.
Exporters immediately criticised the move, saying the refund was too low to allow substantial exports.
Traders pointed out that EU wheat had now to compete on world markets against Argentine wheat worth $130-133 fob.

They calculated that to meet competition from Argentina in traditional EU markets, the EU would need to sell its wheat at around $140 per tonne fob. This would translate into an EU export rebate of 27-30 Ecus.
"The EU's behaviour makes no sense. We are locked out of most business deals," said one trader, adding it was "unbelievable" that Bulgaria was now buying Argentine wheat.
Exporters said U.S. wheat could no longer be the benchmark used to calculate the level of EU refunds. The U.S. had already sold more than 90 pct of its soft red winter crop.
Soft red winter wheat for January was now worth a nominal 150-$156 per tonne.
The main threat to EU exports comes from bumper Argentine and Australian crops that are just starting to hit world markets.
Australia, whose harvest becomes available in December, has already sold 3.5-4 milion tonnes of soft wheat out of potential exports of of 18 million tonnes, traders said.
Canada has already sold between nine and ten million tonnes of wheat.
In the first five months of the 1996/97 season (July/June) the EU sold around 3.8 million tonnes of soft wheat grain out of potential exports of 12 million tonnes.
But some exporters now put that target closer to 10 million due to the EU's reluctance to compete against other origins.
EU grain industry sources, however, said the Commission was doing its utmost to limit the level of EU wheat refunds while keeping the export flow going.
They said the Commission was right in not getting "too uptight" about competition from Argentina, a country that does not subsidise exports.
They also welcomed an EU decision on Thursday to set a special refund of 28 Ecus per tonne on wheat exports to a target group of African nations.
"That's a good move," one source said. The measure had been expected after a previous EU attempt to provide relief to the same group of hard-pressed nations failed earlier this month.
